learningObjectives.title: Types and methods of data transmission

questions.q: A data packet is typically divided into which three parts?
options: Header, payload and trailer
Start bit, data and stop bit
Source, checksum and route
Key, message and signature
questions.explain: A packet has a header (control data such as addresses), a payload (the actual data) and a trailer (which marks the end and often carries error-checking data).

questions.q: How is data sent in serial transmission?
options: One bit at a time down a single wire
Several bits at a time down multiple wires
One byte at a time in both directions
Two bits at a time down two wires
questions.explain: Serial transmission sends bits one after another down a single channel.

questions.q: Which statement describes half-duplex data transmission?
options: Data can be sent in both directions, but not at the same time
Data can be sent in one direction only
Data can be sent in both directions at the same time
Data is sent several bits at a time
questions.explain: In half-duplex, transmission is possible both ways but only one direction at any given moment, such as a walkie-talkie.

questions.q: What does the abbreviation USB stand for?
options: Universal Serial Bus
Unified System Bus
Universal System Buffer
United Serial Backbone
questions.explain: USB stands for Universal Serial Bus, a common serial connection standard.

questions.q: Why is parallel transmission generally only suitable over short distances?
options: Bits can arrive out of step (skew), causing errors over longer distances
It can only ever send data in one direction
It uses a single wire that cannot carry signals far
It has no way of detecting transmission errors
questions.explain: Over longer distances the bits sent along the separate wires can arrive at slightly different times (skew), so parallel is used only for short distances.

questions.q: Which situation is an example of full-duplex transmission?
options: A telephone call where both people can speak and be heard at once
A keyboard sending key presses to a computer
A walkie-talkie where only one person talks at a time
A signal sent from a sensor to a monitoring computer
questions.explain: Full-duplex allows data to travel in both directions simultaneously, as in a telephone conversation.

questions.q: What is a key feature of packet switching?
options: Packets can travel to their destination along different routes
All packets must follow one fixed physical path
Data is never split into smaller units
The whole message is sent as a single continuous stream
questions.explain: In packet switching a message is split into packets that can each take different routes and are reassembled at the destination.

questions.q: A company needs to send data reliably over a long distance between two buildings. Which method of transmission is most appropriate?
options: Serial transmission, because it avoids skew over long distances
Parallel transmission, because it is always faster
Simplex parallel transmission over eight wires
Half-duplex parallel transmission to reduce errors
questions.explain: Serial transmission is preferred over long distances because it avoids the skew problems that affect parallel transmission.

questions.q: What is the purpose of a parity bit?
options: To make the total number of 1s in a byte match an agreed odd or even count
To encrypt the byte before it is sent
To store the address of the destination device
To increase the speed of transmission
questions.explain: A parity bit is set so the number of 1s in the byte is odd (odd parity) or even (even parity), allowing single-bit errors to be detected.

questions.q: What is a checksum?
options: A value calculated from a block of data and recalculated at the receiving end to check for errors
An extra copy of the data sent for comparison
A key used to decrypt received data
The final digit of an entered number such as a barcode
questions.explain: A checksum is calculated from the data before sending, transmitted with it, then recalculated at the receiver; a mismatch indicates an error.

questions.q: What does ARQ stand for in data transmission?
options: Automatic Repeat reQuest
Automatic Response Queue
Acknowledged Return Query
Assured Retransmission Quota
questions.explain: ARQ stands for Automatic Repeat reQuest, which uses acknowledgements and timeouts to trigger retransmission of faulty data.

questions.q: The 7-bit data value 1110000 is to be transmitted using even parity. What is the value of the parity bit?
questions.explain: The data contains three 1s; with even parity the parity bit must be 1 to make the total number of 1s (four) even.

questions.q: A single parity check is used on a byte. Which error will it FAIL to detect?
options: Two bits within the byte change value
A single bit changes from 0 to 1
A single bit changes from 1 to 0
The parity bit itself is corrupted
questions.explain: If two bits change, the count of 1s can stay odd or even as expected, so a single parity check cannot detect the error.

questions.q: How does an echo check detect transmission errors?
options: The received data is sent back to the sender and compared with the original
A calculated value is recomputed at the receiving end
An extra digit is added to the end of the data
The number of 1s in each byte is counted
questions.explain: In an echo check the receiver sends the data back to the sender, which compares it with what was sent; any difference indicates an error.

questions.q: Where is a check digit typically used?
options: As an extra digit at the end of a number such as a barcode or ISBN
As a bit added to each byte during serial transmission
As a value stored in a packet header
As a key shared between sender and receiver
questions.explain: A check digit is an additional digit placed at the end of a code (such as a barcode or ISBN) to detect data entry or reading errors.

questions.q: What is the main purpose of encryption?
options: To make data meaningless to anyone who intercepts it without authorisation
To detect errors that occur during transmission
To compress data so it takes less time to send
To split data into packets for routing
questions.explain: Encryption scrambles data so that if it is intercepted it cannot be understood without the correct key.

questions.q: What are the correct terms for data before and after encryption?
options: Plaintext before, ciphertext after
Ciphertext before, plaintext after
Payload before, checksum after
Cleartext before, keytext after
questions.explain: Data before encryption is called plaintext, and the scrambled result is called ciphertext.

questions.q: Which statement best describes symmetric encryption?
options: The same key is used to encrypt and to decrypt the data
A public key encrypts and a private key decrypts
No key is needed to decrypt the data
A different key is generated for every single byte
questions.explain: Symmetric encryption uses one shared secret key for both encryption and decryption.

questions.q: Which pair of keys is used in asymmetric encryption?
options: A public key and a private key
Two identical shared keys
A parity key and a checksum key
A plaintext key and a ciphertext key
questions.explain: Asymmetric encryption uses a public key (shared openly) and a private key (kept secret) that are mathematically related.

questions.q: A message is encrypted using the recipient's public key. Which key is needed to decrypt it?
options: The recipient's private key
The sender's public key
The recipient's public key
The sender's private key
questions.explain: In asymmetric encryption, data encrypted with a recipient's public key can only be decrypted with the matching private key held by the recipient.
